questions: Is the involuntary eye closure affecting both eyes?
Do the episodes consist of repeated forceful blinking or spasms rather than the eyes simply remaining closed?
Are the episodes triggered or worsened by bright light, wind, reading, watching television, stress, or fatigue?
Can you voluntarily keep your eyes open during an episode?
Do you feel an urge or discomfort that is relieved by closing your eyes?
Are there involuntary movements of the mouth, jaw, tongue, or neck at the same time?
Is one side of your face affected more than the other?
Do the movements continue while you are asleep?
Have you had eye pain, redness, itching, discharge, or a gritty sensation?
Has your vision become blurred or otherwise changed during these episodes?
Have you recently started, stopped, or changed the dose of any medication?
Do you take medications for nausea, psychiatric conditions, seizures, or Parkinson’s disease?
Have you had facial weakness, numbness, limb weakness, difficulty speaking, or loss of consciousness?
Have you ever had similar involuntary movements elsewhere in your body?

results: 1. Comprehensive movement-disorders neurological examination, including observation at rest, during conversation, reading, sustained eye opening, voluntary blinking, forceful eye closure, mouth opening, speaking, and walking
cranial nerve examination: involuntary blepharospasm with perioral and jaw dystonic spasms, provoked by speech and eating; otherwise normal
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
distribution of the dystonia (focal, segmental, generalized): SEGMENTAL - eyelids plus perioral and jaw muscles, not isolated blepharospasm
2. Examination for sensory tricks and task-specific modulation of the eyelid and orofacial movements
action specificity and task dependence: spasms provoked by speech and eating
3. Slit-lamp examination and fluorescein ocular-surface examination
4. Brain MRI with and without contrast, including the brainstem and basal ganglia
5. Video recording of the abnormal movements during spontaneous activity and standardized activation maneuvers
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Idiopathic segmental cranial dystonia (Meige syndrome: bilateral blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia)

1. Tardive dyskinesia/dystonia
2. Hemifacial spasm with associated oromandibular movements
3. Functional movement disorder presenting as segmental cranial dystonia
